questions.title: Large molecules leave the cell by exocytosis
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Physiology > Cell Physiology > Membrane Transport
questions.question: Large molecules that cannot pass through membrane channels are typically moved out of the cell by which process?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endocytosis moves material into the cell by inward budding of the membrane, the opposite direction from exporting a large molecule out of the cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Simple diffusion applies only to small, nonpolar, lipid-soluble molecules crossing directly through the bilayer, not to large molecules, which cannot fit through the hydrophobic core at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Facilitated diffusion moves a specific small-to-moderate solute through a dedicated carrier or channel protein; it is not a mechanism suited to exporting a large molecule.
explanations.D: Correct. A large molecule is packaged inside a membrane-bound vesicle, typically by the Golgi apparatus, and the vesicle then migrates to the plasma membrane and fuses with it, releasing its contents outside the cell — this vesicular export process is exocytosis, and it requires energy. Exocytosis is used both for continuous (constitutive) secretion and for signal-triggered (regulated) secretion, such as calcium-triggered neurotransmitter release at a synapse.

questions.learning_objective: State that large molecules unable to cross the membrane through a channel or carrier are exported from the cell by exocytosis — vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane.
